## METHODOLOGY
This investigation included 169 untreated patients referred to our outpatient clinic for ABPM. Arterial hypertension was diagnosed according to current guidelines. 13 Exclusion criteria were antihypertensive treatment, symptoms or signs of heart failure, coronary artery disease, previous cerebrovascular events, atrial fibrillation, congenital heart disease, heart valve disease (more than mild), neoplastic disease, liver cirrhosis, kidney failure, and endocrine diseases (including type 2 diabetes mellitus).

Anthropometric measures (height, weight) and laboratory analyses (level of fasting glucose, blood creatinine, total cholesterol, and triglycerides) were obtained from all of the patients included in the study. Body mass index (BMI) and body surface area (BSA) were calculated for each patient.

The study was approved by the local ethics committee, and informed consent was obtained from all participants.

## Clinic BP Measurement and 24-Hour ABPM
All participants underwent 24-hour ABPM according to current guidelines. 13 Clinic arterial BP values were obtained by aneroid manometer in the morning hours by calculating the average value of the three consecutive measurements in the sitting position, taken within an interval of 5 to 10 minutes, after the patient had rested for at least 5 minutes in that position.

The noninvasive 24-hour ABPM was performed on the nondominant arm, using a Schiller BR-102 plus system BP monitor (Schiller AG, Baar, Switzerland). The device was programmed to obtain BP readings at 20-minute intervals during the day (7 AM -11 PM) and at 30-minute intervals during the night (11 PM -7 AM). Nighttime BP was defined as the average of BPs from the time patients went to bed until the time they got out of bed, and daytime BP was defined as the average of BPs recorded during the rest of the day. The recording was then analyzed to obtain 24-hour average systolic BP (SBP) and diastolic BP (DBP). When the readings exceeded at least 70% of the total readings programmed for the testing period, the recording was considered valid and satisfactory.

MH was defined as a normal clinic BP (SBP < 140 mm Hg and DBP < 90 mm Hg) measured on at least two separate occasions associated with a 24-hour ambulatory SBP > 130 mm Hg and/or DBP > 80 mm Hg. On the other hand, patients with sustained hypertension had an elevated clinic SBP of 140 mm Hg together with a 24-hour ambulatory SBP ≥ 130 mm Hg or DBP ≥ 80 mm Hg.

## Echocardiography
Echocardiographic examinations were performed using a commercially available Vivid 7 device (GE Vingmed, Horten, Norway). Reported values of all two-dimensional echocardiographic (2DE) parameters were obtained as the average value of three consecutive cardiac cycles. LV dimensions were measured according to joined guidelines of the American and European societies of echocardiography. 14 Relative wall thickness was calculated according to the formula: (2 9 posterior wall thickness)/LV end-diastolic diameter. Posterior wall thickness was measured at end-diastole. LV ejection fraction (EF) was calculated by using the biplane method. LV mass (LVM) was calculated by using the corrected method described in the joined guidelines of the American and European societies of echocardiography and indexed for BSA. 14

Doppler assessment of transmitral flow was obtained in the apical four-chamber view according to the guidelines. 15 Tissue Doppler imaging was used to obtain LV myocardial velocities in the apical four-chamber view, with a sample volume placed at the septal and lateral segments of the mitral annulus during early diastole (e 0 ). The average of the peak early diastolic relaxation velocity (e 0 ) of the septal and lateral mitral annulus was calculated, and the E/e 0 ratio was computed.

text:
## RESULTS
All three groups were of similar age and sex distribution (Table I). There was no difference in BMI, although BSA was somewhat higher in the MH and sustained hypertensive groups than in controls (Table I). Heart rate was similar between all groups. Clinic BP was similar between controls and the MH group, and significantly higher in the sustained hypertensive group (Table I). On the other hand, 24-hour BP was significantly higher in the MH and sustained hypertensive groups than in controls (Table I). Plasma glucose and creatinine levels were similar throughout the groups, whereas cholesterol and triglyceride levels were higher in the MH and hypertensive groups.

## Echocardiographic Measurements
LV diameters were similar among the groups, while LV interventricular, posterior wall, and relative wall thicknesses were significantly higher in the MH and sustained hypertensive patients than in controls (Table II). LVMI progressively increased from normotensive across MH patients to hypertensive patients (Table II). There was no difference in LV 2DE EF between all three groups. Mitral E/A ratio decreased and mitral E/e' ratio increased gradually from normotensive to sustained hypertensive (Table II).

text:
## LA Phasic Function
All LAVs (maximum, minimum, and pre-A) and corresponding LAV indexes progressively and significantly increased from normotensive controls to sustained hypertensive patients (Table III).

There was no significant difference in total LAV between groups. Total LA EF, which describes LA reservoir function, was lower in MH and sustained hypertensive patients than in normotensive controls (Table III and Figure). Passive LAV was lower in hypertensive patients than in controls and MH patients, and passive LA EF, a parameter of LA conduit function, gradually declined from normotensive controls, throughout MH, to sustained hypertensive patients (Table III and Figure). Active LAV and active LA EF gradually increased from normotensives to sustained hypertensive patients (Table III and Figure).

Total and positive LA longitudinal strain gradually decreased from controls to sustained hypertensive patients, whereas negative LA longitudinal strain was higher in MH and sustained hypertensives than in normotensive controls (Table III and Figure).

LA stiffness index significantly and progressively increased from normotensive controls, across MH, to sustained hypertensive patients (Table III).
